# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 34 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 34 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_034_page_001.jpg

---

## Mandate 5, Chapter 2 — Against Anger

**1** "Remove anger and bitterness from yourself, and you will be found in full possession of your senses with the Holy Spirit. **2** Be on guard against anger, for it is an evil and harmful spirit. See how anger destroys the minds of those with incomplete faith — and indeed even the most righteous. **3** For anger is thoroughly destructive, for it is the instrument of the devil. **4** Free yourself from anger by replacing it with long-suffering. For where bitterness is, death is there also, and the bitter person will not inherit the kingdom of God. **5** Those who are angry are mastered by the devil and cast away from the Lord, and they become corrupted. **6** But those who are patient resist the evil one — and in resisting they gain power over him and overcome him. The patient person will live to God, and the long-suffering person will overcome the evil one." **7** I said, "Sir, I would like to understand the working of anger — how it destroys the minds of God's servants." **8** He said, "Even the most gentle person, when anger overtakes him, becomes very bitter very quickly — because of a wife, a child, a servant, a friend, a fellow believer, or some business transaction. He becomes arrogant and sharp in his speech. **9** After that, complete bitterness overtakes him, and he remembers neither God nor Christ the Lord, and he speaks words of injustice and lawlessness, piling evil upon evil. **10** This is why the patience of God is necessary: patience drives anger away and destroys it utterly from the person's heart."

---

### Council Notes

Mandate 5.2 moves from the pneumatological theory (ch. 33) to the practical phenomenology of anger. The description of the anger-spiral (v. 8-10) is one of the most acute psychological observations in early Christian literature:

1. Gentle person receives minor provocation
2. Rapid onset of bitterness
3. Arrogance and sharp speech
4. Total bitterness
5. **Forgetting God and Christ** — the spiritual amnesia of anger
6. Lawless, unjust speech

The phrase "remembers neither God nor Christ the Lord" (v. 9) is remarkable — it suggests that the deepest identity of the believer (their knowledge of and relationship with God) is temporarily obliterated by sustained anger.

The antidote is "the patience of God" — not just human patience, but divine makrothymia working within the person. The cure matches the disease: as anger is a demonic spirit, so patience is a divine quality.
